waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: The Stuart Lake Trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 7601, which leaves Icicle Creek Road; the parking area is at about 3,400 ft and Trail #1599 starts there. Plan the day from the car either as a single car-to-car push, which runs about 13-14 hours for a fit party, or as a backpack in to camp at Colchuck Lake — camping needs an Enchantments overnight permit, so sort that out before you drive up.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction and turn left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, cross Mountaineer Creek and grind up the rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft.

waypoints.name: Dragontail Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: Go around the lake's west shore to its south end, boulder-hop onto the crest of the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine and follow it south toward the northwest face to the band of orange rock low on the wall. Cross the moat onto 4th-class ledges through the orange band, then climb the arete's crack and dihedral pitches and the ridge crest and sandy gully to the summit.

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass
waypoints.directions: Head down the loose sandy gully shared with the top of Backbone Ridge, downclimb or boot-ski the upper Snow Creek Glacier snowfield where it remains, then traverse east to Aasgard Pass.

road.name: Icicle Road, Eightmile Road (FR 7600) and FR 7601 to the Stuart Lake Trailhead
road.status: Gravel and steep, washboarded later in the season; high clearance recommended, 4x4 advised. Closed to vehicles every winter.
road.driveNote: Take Icicle Road out of Leavenworth for roughly 8.5 mi to the Eightmile Road (FR 7600) turnoff on the left, then stay right onto FR 7601 and follow it about 4 mi, past the Eightmile Trailhead, to where it ends. The lot is small; once it fills, park only on the side of the road the signs permit, because cars in no-parking zones are ticketed.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599)
waypoints.note: Start of the Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass approach, at about 3,400 ft. The Snow Lakes Trailhead is the longer, lower alternative into the same basin.
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive about 8.4 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 7601 and follow the rough, potholed dirt road about 3.7 miles to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park; day trips need the free self-issued Enchantments day-use permit at the trailhead, and overnight stays need a quota permit.

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass
waypoints.directions: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, turn left, cross Mountaineer Creek and switchback 1.6 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then climb Aasgard Pass, about 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree and dirt, staying climber's left of the cliff bands, to the 7,841-ft pass.

waypoints.name: Core Enchantments
waypoints.directions: From the pass, drop gently east into the upper Core past Tranquil and Isolation Lakes and follow the cairned path down through the chain of lakes to the camps in the central basin.

waypoints.name: West ridge notch
waypoints.directions: From the basin camps, take the path toward Prusik Pass that leaves the west shore of Perfection Lake and climb north over granite to the pass, where the West Ridge begins.

waypoints.name: Prusik Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb about four pitches: a long first pitch up a wide crack in a band of white rock onto the crest, then along the ridge to a slung-block belay below the 5.7 friction-slab crux with an old fixed pin, and a finishing pitch by a finger crack or a 5.7 off-width to the summit.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda (Ingalls Way) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-9737 off North Fork Teanaway River Rd; small lot fills fast in summer, Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From Cle Elum, head northeast on SR-970 about 5 miles, turn onto the Teanaway River Road and follow it roughly 23 miles to the road end. The small lot fills fast on summer weekends — a Northwest Forest Pass is required and there is a self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass with the first open view of Mount Stuart and the Ingalls Peaks; forks here, stay left/climber's-path toward Lake Ingalls rather than dropping right into Headlight Basin.
waypoints.directions: Take the Ingalls Way trail and stay left at the fork around 5,600 ft. Three miles of steady climbing brings you to Ingalls Pass, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls Peaks come into view all at once. Fork again here: stay left on the climber's path toward Lake Ingalls rather than dropping right into Headlight Basin.

waypoints.name: Lake Ingalls
waypoints.note: Last reliable water before the summit scramble; camping and campfires are prohibited immediately around the lake to protect the fragile alpine basin, so treat/carry water here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse from the pass to Lake Ingalls, about a mile. This is the last reliable water before the summit, so fill and treat here — camping and campfires are prohibited around the lake to protect the basin.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Col (notch between South and North/main peaks)
waypoints.note: Scramble up slabs, talus and boulders from the lake to this notch below Dogtooth Spire; this is where the roped South Ridge route begins, distinct from the easier North Ridge to South Peak.
waypoints.directions: From the lake, scramble slabs, talus and boulders up to the notch between the North and South peaks, below Dogtooth Spire. Expect snow on this section in June and early July. This notch is where the roped South Ridge begins, and it is a different objective from the easier North Ridge scramble to the South Peak.

waypoints.name: Dogtooth Crags traverse
waypoints.note: Exposed traverse along the right side of the Dogtooth Crags on broken rock and slabs leading to the base bench; loose blocks and route-finding in fog are the main dangers here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the right-hand side of the Dogtooth Crags on broken rock and slabs. Loose blocks are the main hazard, and this is the section people lose in fog — it is worth noting your line on the way in so you can reverse it.

waypoints.name: Bench below the red slab (start of roped pitches)
waypoints.note: Broad bench just below a distinctive large red slab; from the notch descend/traverse about 100 ft west to the base of a friction slab and rope up for the 3-pitch 5.4 ridge climb.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, descend and traverse roughly 100 ft west to the broad bench under the distinctive large red slab. Rope up here: the route is three pitches at 5.4, generally good rock with a few 5.2-5.3 moves and real exposure. The first pitch takes an obvious crack for close to a full rope length to a belay at a fixed piton on the slab.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Peak (North/main summit)
waypoints.note: True summit of Ingalls Peak; exposed but well-protected 5.4 climbing gains the top, descend by rappelling the route back to the col and reversing the approach.
waypoints.directions: Three pitches gain the true summit — exposed but well protected. Descend by rappelling the line you climbed, which goes in three raps on two 60 m ropes, or four on a single 60 m, using the same anchors, then reverse the scramble to the lake and the trail. Budget 3-4 hours for the approach and 3-5 hours for the climb; by August the whole basin gets hot and there is no shade above the lake.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk; $5/day or NW Forest Pass, overnight Enchantment Permit Area reservation required May 15-Oct 31.
waypoints.directions: Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR-7601 off Icicle Creek Road, about 3,400 ft. Self-issue day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk; $5/day or a Northwest Forest Pass. Staying overnight needs an Enchantment Permit Area reservation between 15 May and 31 October, which is a lottery.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake trail split
waypoints.note: Trail forks after paralleling Mountaineer Creek; bear left (south) onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, which climbs switchbacks the rest of the way.
waypoints.directions: The trail parallels Mountaineer Creek for two and a half miles before forking. Bear left, south, onto the Colchuck Lake Trail — the Stuart Lake Trail carries straight on. From the split it is switchbacks the rest of the way.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established backcountry campsites along the shore; Colchuck Glacier and the Colchuck-Dragontail col are visible across the lake.
waypoints.directions: Climb the switchbacks to the lake at about 5,560 ft. Reliable water and established shoreline campsites; from here you can read the whole objective across the water — the Colchuck Glacier and the col between Colchuck and Dragontail.

waypoints.name: Lateral moraine crest above the lake's south/west shore
waypoints.note: Leave the talus for the moraine crest early; the slopes beneath it are loose scree and much worse on the way down.
waypoints.directions: Work around the lake and up the talus on the south-west side, then climb onto the crest of the lateral moraine at the first reasonable spot. Below the crest the ground is loose, shifting scree, far worse to descend than to climb.

waypoints.name: Toe of Colchuck Glacier
waypoints.note: Rope up or don crampons here; snow-covered and non-crevassed early season but turns to bare blue ice by late summer when crampons won't bite.
waypoints.directions: The moraine leads to the glacier's toe. Put crampons on here and take the axe out. The glacier is receding and effectively crevasse-free, so many parties do not rope up — but it is snow-covered early season and turns to bare, hard ice by late summer, when crampons stop biting well and it becomes the crux of the day rather than a walk.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Col (Banshee Pass)
waypoints.note: Saddle between Colchuck and Dragontail peaks reached via the glacier's east/left lobe, steepening to roughly 100 ft of 40-degree snow just below the col.
waypoints.directions: Climb the glacier's east/left lobe toward the col — roughly 1,800 ft of gain from the base of the gravel rib. There is usually a good switchbacking bootpack. The headwall immediately below the col is the steepest ground on the route, around 40 degrees for the last hundred feet or so.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Peak
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scramble northwest/west from the col to the true summit; watch for loose blocks on the final ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the col, scramble north-west to the summit: short, low-exposure high Class 2 to easy Class 3 on mixed rock and dirt. Early in the season this last section holds snow, which makes it harder rather than easier. Reverse the route to descend — most of the day's risk is in downclimbing the glacier when it has softened, and in the loose moraine slopes if you drift off the crest.

waypoints.name: Tucquala Meadows Trailhead
waypoints.note: FS 4330 (Cle Elum Valley Rd), about 11 mi past Salmon La Sac. Standard access for Peggys Pond via Cathedral Pass Trail #1345 to Cathedral Pass, continuing to Mount Daniel's SE slopes/Daniel Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drive up the Cle Elum River valley on Forest Service Road 4330 (Cle Elum Valley Road), about 11 miles past Salmon La Sac, to its end at the trailhead, 3,370 feet. The access road is rough gravel and is best driven with a high-clearance or 4x4 vehicle.

waypoints.name: Peggys Pond
waypoints.directions: Take the Cathedral Rock Trail #1345, which crosses the Cle Elum River on a bridge and climbs past Squaw Lake to Cathedral Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail, about 4.5 miles. Follow the PCT briefly toward Deep Lake; at the first switchback down, take the spur to Peggys Pond, about half a mile of steep, narrow path along ledges with sheer drop-offs and loose rock.

waypoints.name: Mount Daniel (true/West Summit)
waypoints.directions: Follow braided boot paths northwest then west across heather and talus, gaining about 1,500 ft in a mile to the broad southeast ridge near 7,000 ft, with the Hyas Creek Glacier on your right and Circle Lake below on your left. Traverse climbers' trail and scree below the East Summit to the 7,600-ft saddle, then cross loose talus, snow and the rocky glacier margin to the West Summit, staying on rock off the glacier ice.
